summary: Suggests a simple way for delivering wireless messages, one-way and two-way, to appropriate receiving devices such as pagers. It describes version 3 of the Simple Network Paging Protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1861 defines the Simple Network Paging Protocol, a way to send a short text message to a pager over a network connection. The sender types a few short commands, such as the pager's number, the message text and SEND, and the server answers with a three digit code. Version 3 adds two-way paging, where the sender can ask whether the message was delivered, whether it was read, and what the recipient replied.

questions: how to send a page over the internet
how does the simple network paging protocol work
what does snpp level 3 two-way do
why not use email for paging
subtitle: A line-based, SMTP-like protocol for pushing a page to a paging terminal and, in version 3, getting replies back.

tldr.problem: Pages had to be delivered by modem and telephone line, or by email, which is reliable but cannot report a problem straight away and cannot carry a reply from the pager.
tldr.mechanism: SNPP defines a session of short commands, such as the pager number, the message text and SEND, with three digit reply codes, plus optional parameters for service level, coverage area and delayed delivery, and a level three extension that returns a tag and a code for polling delivery and reply status.
tldr.outcome: Gateways and client software for the protocol were in commercial use at paging companies when the memo was written, although reviewers at the IETF preferred to have handled the same need with extensions to SMTP.

facts.label: Service level range
facts.value: Ideally an integer between 0 and 11 inclusive

today: RFC 1861 is an Informational memo published in October 1995, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It revises RFC 1645 by adding the level three two-way extensions, and the memo notes that at the time of publication the TME standard it was written for was still not finalized. Its security section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

sections.title: What SNPP Is For
sections.content:
The intent of the Simple Network Paging Protocol is to provide a standard whereby pages can be delivered to individual paging terminals. The most obvious benefit is the elimination of the need for modems and phone lines to produce alphanumeric pages, and the added ease of delivery of pages to terminals in other cities or countries. The benefits of the Internet become more real as paging moves towards acknowledgment-based messaging such as ReFLEX paging, where it may be impossible to accurately predict the costs of telecommunications services such as 1-800 numbers.

Radio paging is more complicated than it looks. A page entered by dialling a number on a telephone, or typed into an input device, must end up at a paging terminal somewhere, and in most cases this delivery is made using TAP, the Telocator Alphanumeric input Protocol, also known as IXO. TAP can be a somewhat convoluted protocol, using older style ASCII control characters and a non-standard checksumming routine to help validate the data. Even though TAP is widely used, there are plans to move to a more flexible standard protocol, TME, the Telocator Message Entry Protocol, and the level two enhancements of SNPP are intended for use with it.

Two-way paging opens up new areas of unpredictability, the most pronounced being subscriber response time: although delivery from host to subscriber and the receipt of acknowledgments happen predictably, it is impossible to know when the subscriber will physically pull the unit out, read the message and respond. Conducting such transactions online using a phone line could be cost prohibitive, especially an 800-number, which makes the Internet attractive because of its generally usage insensitive nature. The final user function is nonetheless quite simple, to deliver a page from point of origin to someone's beeper, and that simple, real-time function is what the base protocol addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: SNPP exists to get a text message from a computer to a pager. Using the Internet avoids a modem and a phone line, and it avoids the awkward cost of an 800 number when the pager can reply.

sections.title: Why Not Just Use Email and SMTP
sections.content:
Email, while quite reliable, is not always timely. The memo's example is deferred messaging when a gateway is down. Mary Ghoti sends a message to Zaphod Beeblebrox's beeper, and her company's gateway to the Internet is down, so the message is deferred. Mary is not notified, because her message has not actually failed to reach its destination. Three hours later the link is restored and the message is sent, but if the page concerned a meeting that was supposed to happen two hours ago there are administrative details to sort out.

If Mary had used her SNPP client, or simply telnetted to the SNPP gateway, she would have discovered the network problem immediately, and could have invoked plan B and telephoned the pager. The difference is not page delivery but the immediate notification of a problem that affects the message. Standard email and SMTP cannot be positively guaranteed between all nodes at all times, which makes them less desirable for emergency or urgent paging, and could place a service provider in an uncomfortable position with a client who has just received an emergency page six hours too late.

A separate protocol also gives the sender absolute flexibility over what is sent to the pager. In the paging arena, where messages go to alphanumeric pagers, it is less desirable to send the recipient the general header lines of a standard SMTP message: much of the information is useless, possibly redundant, and a waste of precious radio bandwidth. A service provider implementing an SMTP gateway should therefore parse out the needed information, such as the sender and possibly the subject, which generally means less control over content and format by the message originator. SNPP instead provides a clean way to send a message, as written, to the recipient's pager, and it is simpler for a manual telnet session than hacking a mail message into a gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail that cannot be delivered is often queued rather than reported, so a page that arrives six hours late is no use in an emergency. A paging protocol reports the problem straight away and sends only the text the sender wrote, with no wasted radio bandwidth spent on mail headers.

sections.title: Commands and Reply Codes
sections.content:
SNPP is a sequence of commands and replies. The input commands, of which the first four characters are significant, solicit server responses that fall into categories: 2xx successful, continue; 3xx begin DATA input; 4xx failed with the connection terminated; and 5xx failed but continue the session. Version 3 adds 7xx for an unsuccessful two-way transaction but the session continues, 8xx for a successful two-way transaction, and 9xx for a successful queued two-way transaction. The first character of every response code is a digit indicating the category, and the text after the code may be altered to suit individual applications.

The session interaction, especially at level one, is simple. The client opens the connection, the server issues a 220 message showing it is willing to accept SNPP commands, the client passes the pager ID and the message and issues a SEND command, and the server feeds the information to the paging terminal, gathers a response and reports success or failure to the client.

The general response codes are set out in the memo. Code 214 prefixes each line of a multi-line help message and is terminated by a 250 OK. Code 218 prefixes a single line of information and has no terminator. Code 250 is a general positive acknowledgment that a command was processed successfully. Code 421 is shown just before the server terminates a connection, for administrative or technical reasons. Code 500 is a fail but continue code used when an illegal command is entered, and 503 says the information has already been entered. Codes 550 and 554 report a failed command with the session allowed to continue, where 550 is an administrative failure such as an invalid pager ID or illegal parameter, and 554 a technical reason such as a gateway down or equipment failure. Code 552 is sent in response to the entry of the n+1st item when the server permits only n items in a category.

The level one commands are PAGEr, which submits a pager ID for inclusion in the next messaging transaction, MESSage, which specifies a single line message, RESEt, which clears already entered information and resets the session to the state of a freshly opened connection, SEND, which finalizes the current message transaction and processes the page, QUIT, which terminates the session, and the optional HELP, which displays the commands valid on the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends short commands and the server answers with a three digit code whose first digit says what happened: two means fine, four means the session is over, five means the command failed but you can carry on. Each command, such as giving the pager number or the message text, has its own set of possible answers.

sections.title: Example Transactions
sections.content:
The memo gives three worked examples. A typical level one connection opens the connection and receives 220 SNPP Gateway Ready, sends PAGE 5551212 and gets 250 Pager ID Accepted, sends MESS with the message text and gets 250 Message OK, sends SEND and gets 250 Message Sent OK, and ends with QUIT and 221 OK, Goodbye.

The level two example sends one message to two pagers, with pager-specific options chosen before each PAGEr command: COVE 2 selects an alternate coverage area for the first pager, and HOLD 9401152300 -0600 asks for delayed delivery for the second. A subject line is set with SUBJ, and the message body follows a DATA command, which the server answers with 354 Begin Input, End With '.', and the client ends its input with a line holding a single period.

The level three example is a two-way transaction. It begins with the 2WAY command and ends with a SEND command, and along the way the client asks for the pager's status, for a read acknowledgment and for multiple choice replies to be enabled. The server answers 850 Unit online, and after the send returns 860 00321 1234 Message Delivered, where the 860 series means the initial message was delivered and the requested actions are still outstanding.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo shows three exchanges end to end: a simple one-way page, a page to two pagers with different options for each, and a two-way page where the sender waits to hear what the recipient replies.

sections.title: Level 2 Extensions
sections.content:
Level two adds a minimum extension and a set of optional ones. DATA is an alternate form of the MESSage command that allows a message of multiple lines to be delivered to the paging terminal, and its function is similar to the DATA command implemented in SMTP. Only one DATA or MESSage command should be allowed before a SEND. The optional commands mirror the added functionality built into the Telocator Message Entry protocol, there is no requirement to implement all of them, and a request for an invalid function should return a 500 Function Not Implemented error. The memo notes that at the time of publication the TME standard was still not finalized.

LOGIn specifies a session login ID and optional password, used to validate the person attempting to access the paging terminal; if no LOGIn command is issued, anonymous user status is assumed. The level two PAGEr command adds a password or PIN for validation or feature access. The option commands LEVEl, ALERt, COVErage and HOLDuntil each set a parameter submitted with the next PAGEr command, and those parameters reset to their defaults once that PAGEr command has been processed. This option-option-option-go scheme makes it possible to give each recipient their own settings while sending the same message to each.

LEVEl takes a service level, ideally an integer between 0 and 11 inclusive, where 0 is Priority, 1 is Normal and the default, 2 to 7 give delivery windows from five minutes up to twenty four hours, and 8 to 11 are carrier specific. ALERt overrides whether the subscriber is alerted on receipt of a message, either 0 DoNotAlert or 1 Alert. COVErage overrides the subscriber's default coverage area with an alternate region, either a subscriber-specific one or a carrier-defined region. HOLDuntil asks for delayed delivery of a message until after the time specified, given in local time or with an offset from GMT such as -0600 for Eastern Standard Time. Two message-oriented functions are also optional: CALLerid, which passes the caller identifier as described in TME, and SUBJect, which sets a subject for the next message.
sections.plainLanguage: Level two lets the sender give a message more than one line, sign in to the gateway, and set options for the person receiving it, such as the service level, whether the pager beeps, which area to page in, or delivery after a chosen time. Each option applies to the next pager addressed, then goes back to its default.

sections.title: Level 3 Two-Way Transactions
sections.content:
Level three supports acknowledgment-based paging. One of the more powerful features of ReFLEX-style paging, in addition to confirmed message delivery, is the ability to seed a message with multiple choice responses, so that after viewing the message the recipient can reply with one of the seeded messages, and the sender may elect to receive confirmation when the message is first viewed.

The 2WAY command puts the server into two-way mode for a single transaction, and the server returns to non-2WAY mode when a SEND or a RESEt command completes. PING localizes the field message unit and returns its location and status. EXPTag changes the default expiry time for a queued message; if the message is not delivered in the specified number of hours it is deleted and the status tag is updated to reflect the inability to deliver, with code 760. NOQUEUEing stops the server queueing a message for a pager that is not online, so a PAGEr command then returns a 750 series response, and it must be specified before a PAGEr command. ACKRead switches the read acknowledgment on or off, so that the field message unit returns a message when the subscriber actually views the received message.

RTYPe sets the kind of reply the client will accept: NONE, the default, which permits no reply; YESNO, which seeds a simple yes or no reply; SIMREPLY, which allows only pre-coded replies from the provider's reply base; MULTICHOICE, which allows full multiple choice replies; and TEXT, which allows full text replies generated by the field unit. MCREsponse, issued before the SEND command, seeds the transaction with an acceptable multiple choice response made of a two-byte code and its text, and the number of acceptable responses may be limited by the server.

A successful SEND in two-way mode returns a Message_Tag, which functions as a record locator, and a Pass_Code, which should be a randomly generated PIN code authorizing checks of that tag. The client then uses MSTAtus to check the progression of the transaction, and the replies come in tiers: 86x means the initial message was delivered and the requested actions are outstanding, 87x means intermediate processing is complete and the transaction awaits closure, 88x means the transaction is concluded and no further status changes will take place, and 96x means a queued transaction. The status record carries a Sequence number that rises as the record's status changes, and the date and time in the form YYMMDDHHMMSS+GMT. KTAG kills the message tag after final reading, so the client does not have to wait for the server to expire it.

The memo's security section says only that security issues are not discussed in it. Two of the mechanisms above are worth noting anyway. The PING command notes that because of the sensitive nature of location information the subscriber may elect to have a generic pager located message returned instead of her actual location, which the memo calls ACLU mode. And the Pass_Code returned by SEND should be a randomly generated PIN code that authorizes checks of the Message_Tag.
sections.plainLanguage: Level three lets the sender follow a message all the way. The server hands back a tag for the message and a random code, and the sender polls with them to learn whether the page was delivered, whether it was read, and what the recipient replied. The codes say how far the transaction has got.

items.text: Service level for the next page, ideally an integer from 0 to 11.

items.text: An alternate coverage area for the next page.

items.title: HOLDuntil
items.text: Delayed delivery until a given time, with an optional GMT offset.
